name: Monday Natural Products: Data Warehouse Migration
description: The CFO of Monday Natural Products sponsors the migration from the company's legacy reporting platform to a maintainable data warehouse so leaders can receive faster, consistent information for operational and strategic decisions. Delivery depends on reliable data and subject-matter input from ERP, e-commerce, logistics, and finance teams, and the warehouse must go live within the fixed 14-week window. The client values budget predictability: although the simulation displays a nominal EUR 240,000 budget, management has reserved EUR 30,000 of it as contingency and expects the baseline plan to spend no more than EUR 210,000. Key risks include inconsistent source data, limited stakeholder availability, compressed unit and integration testing, and inadequate knowledge transfer to the support team. You are taking over as project manager and must balance delivery flow, quality, schedule, and transparent cost control.

fragments.title: Initial Project Charter
fragments.body: You are taking over as project manager. Deliver a maintainable warehouse integrating ERP, e-commerce, logistics, and finance data by the end of week 14. Protect current operations, establish data ownership, and plan unit, integration, and acceptance testing plus support-team knowledge transfer. The nominal budget is EUR 240,000; management has reserved EUR 30,000 for contingency, so plan to a EUR 210,000 baseline ceiling.

fragments.title: Week 4 Sponsor Update
fragments.body: A new supplier-data compliance requirement needs traceable transformations and extra validation. At the same time, supplier costs have risen. The sponsor therefore imposes a new EUR 190,000 spending ceiling for the remainder of the project. This is a management constraint, not a change to the simulation's displayed EUR 240,000 nominal budget. Reforecast, protect the fixed go-live, and escalate trade-offs.

fragments.title: Quality and Readiness Briefing
fragments.body: Before go-live, review rejected transformations, unresolved source-data issues, and coverage across ERP, e-commerce, logistics, and finance interfaces. Confirm stakeholder availability for acceptance decisions, preserve enough capacity for integration and regression testing, and schedule documented knowledge-transfer sessions. Recommend corrective action without treating unfinished or untested work as delivered value.

fragments.title: Steering-Committee Review
fragments.body: Present the terminal review to the steering committee. Compare accepted scope, defects, elapsed time, and total cost with the fixed go-live and management's EUR 190,000 spending ceiling, while also reporting the engine's unchanged EUR 240,000 nominal budget. Explain your major trade-off, residual data and operational risks, test evidence, stakeholder acceptance, and whether the support team can operate the warehouse.

questions.prompt: At kickoff, which governance and staffing approach will you adopt for the 14-week migration?

options.label: Fund a cross-functional core team with weekly data-owner decisions
Start lean and add specialists through stage-gate escalation
Front-load scarce specialists, then transition work to the delivery team
Assign interface workstreams to source-system teams with central assurance

feedback_by_option.cross_functional_core: A stable core raises early cost but shortens decisions and supports continuous quality. Weekly owner access can protect schedule and acceptance, provided governance does not become meeting-heavy.
feedback_by_option.lean_escalation: Low initial burn preserves contingency and gives sponsors control. Later approvals or scarce hires may delay work, compress testing, and frustrate stakeholders if escalation thresholds are vague.
feedback_by_option.specialist_frontload: Early expertise can retire hard design risks and improve estimates, at a high initial cost. Schedule and support quality depend on disciplined transfer before specialists leave and owners validating decisions.
feedback_by_option.workstream_ownership: Distributed ownership can deepen interface knowledge and stakeholder commitment while containing central cost. Competing operational priorities may slow delivery or create uneven quality without common standards.

questions.prompt: By week 4, which risks are most important to place on the active watchlist? Select all that merit explicit mitigation.

options.label: Inconsistent source data and unclear ownership
ERP, commerce, logistics, or finance interface changes
Late knowledge transfer to the support team
Uncontrolled growth in reports, rules, or compliance needs
Unit-test shortcuts accumulating as integration debt
Stakeholders disagreeing about dashboard colors and branding
A planned office move disrupting in-person ceremonies

feedback_by_option.data_quality: Profiling, ownership, and acceptance rules consume capacity now but reduce transformation rework, disputed outputs, and late stakeholder rejection.
feedback_by_option.interface_changes: Contract monitoring and change control protect integration. Ignored interface drift can invalidate completed mappings and consume schedule and test budget.
feedback_by_option.scarce_expertise: Named backups and reserved expert time cost money but reduce bottlenecks. Unavailable experts can stall decisions and force lower-quality workarounds.
feedback_by_option.knowledge_transfer: Pairing and documented rehearsals reduce current throughput, yet lower handover and operational risk. Deferring transfer makes support readiness dependent on a few people.
feedback_by_option.scope_growth: A visible change budget and sponsor trade-offs preserve alignment. Quiet additions dilute capacity, push tests later, and obscure the forecast.
feedback_by_option.testing_debt: Tracking skipped tests as debt makes the cost visible. Leaving it unmanaged can create misleading progress and expensive integration defects near go-live.
feedback_by_option.dashboard_branding: Branding disagreement can affect acceptance, but decision time-boxes usually contain it. Compare its likely impact with risks that threaten data correctness or integration.
feedback_by_option.office_move: Location disruption may affect ceremonies, but remote access and scheduling can often mitigate it. Assess evidence before diverting contingency from delivery-critical risks.

questions.prompt: The sponsor has announced the EUR 190,000 spending ceiling. Which immediate response will you authorize?

options.label: Negotiate controlled scope trades while protecting acceptance and compliance
Cut staff evenly across every role and workstream
Hold scope and staffing cost by relying on sustained overtime
Reforecast from accepted work, defects, capacity, and remaining risk

feedback_by_option.scope_negotiation: Explicit trades can align cost and time while protecting critical quality, but stakeholders may lose valued outcomes and negotiations must not delay the fixed date.
feedback_by_option.staff_cuts: Uniform cuts lower forecast cost quickly and appear equitable. They can remove scarce skills, slow interfaces, weaken testing, and leave owners uncertain about accountability.
feedback_by_option.sustained_overtime: Overtime may preserve near-term milestones without immediate hiring cost. Sustained use increases fatigue, defects, turnover risk, and stakeholder doubt about whether the plan is credible.
feedback_by_option.evidence_replan: Evidence exposes the cost-to-complete and supports defensible allocation changes. Analysis takes time and may reveal that scope, risk tolerance, or expectations still require sponsor negotiation.

questions.prompt: Give a go/no-go recommendation. Support it with the current forecast against the EUR 190,000 ceiling, accepted work, unresolved quality or test work, and time remaining to week 14.
Give the steering committee a concise retrospective: connect at least one staffing or allocation decision to delivered scope, elapsed time, total cost, quality, and team sustainability.
